turn_text: You serve on two very important committees in the house with regard to the industry of agriculture and the food supply chain on appropriations and on agriculture. turn_text: Your chamber has a committee that is looking at climate change. And some sea agriculture is a part of the problem and some sea agriculture is a part of the solution by being able to sequester carbon and certainly to give new emphasis to the soil. Where would you point to agriculture in the challenge of climate debate?

Well, this is actually my favorite topic, although I would say it's been kind of pushed aside with everything else that we're all challenged by right now, but I did work for more than a year. on a piece of legislation on climate change, the Agricultural Resilience Act, and I had meetings with tens of, I don't know, 100 different groups from conventional ag, big ag, small ag, environmentalist, everything. And one thing I was really disturbed by, say a year ago was the sense that people had understanding that there's some issues around climate change. And then putting it in very simplistic terms and just saying like, okay, here's how we fix it. We plant a tree and you stop eating meat. And I'm just appalled by that idea that that's all we need to do. We have really looked in our bill about ways to help people understand better the important role of sequestering carbon in the soil, that it's possible in a fully functioning system. You could sequester more carbon in the soil than you do in trees. You know, while we're not talking about that today, We overall understand that there's too much carbon in our atmosphere. We're looking at all different kinds of ways to take some of it out. And I come from the most forested state in the nation. So I'm thrilled to have people talking about trees, sequestering carbon. But I don't want to hear people talking about taking highly productive farmland and planting trees and not understanding that farmers can be great partners in this. That there's too much talk about farmers being the villains. And yes, agriculture can be a contributor to the problems with creating carbon, but we also have the opportunity to help farmers to do more sequester carbon. And the great thing is, we have a lot of conservation programs that already encourage this. We have people out there in the field who have been helping farmers to do more no-till cover crops. This has been moving in this direction, and I think if we prioritize more of our programs to incentivize farmers to do that, if there's more technical support for them to do that, I think that they're going to I mean, we were on a pathway where a lot of the major companies that are buying, we're looking for farmers who are using, you know, good environmental techniques, able to say they were sequestering carbon in the soil. And those companies are saying, well, this is the product we want to buy. This is the corn. These are soybeans because we want to put a label on our product or tell our consumers We're using the best possible tactics here. We also think that farmers should have the opportunity to participate in carbon markets, and that's a much more sophisticated conversation. But we've talked to Secretary Perdue and others. Right now, there are a lot of people in the forestry industry who are able to benefit from using the growth of trees as an offset and get paid for that. And I think, look, a farmer can use every penny they can make out there. And why shouldn't they be a part of these markets? It does require having more sophisticated system to measure how much carbon that you're capturing but there are people in private industry, there are university researchers, there's work being done at the USDA. We just have to come together on some standards and all those things we put into this legislation because in the end we just want to say, hey, farmers can be great partners in this, they can be our future heroes and they're the ones who are also suffering many times from the The downside of climate change, the extreme weather, the flooding, the wildfires, the drought, they're the ones who feel the impact quite a bit and why not say, hey, let's make you our partners and let's see how you can benefit financially from doing the right thing.
